title: Captain Zythienne
type: NPC · Zarathian captain, military advocate and civic candidate
dek: A commander who speaks of peace while preparing for further war, mourns his son, honors covert service and asks what duty should demand of others.

body:
Captain Zythienne is a military figure and public advocate for Zarathis. He celebrates courage, but speaks openly of the grief his own household carries. His history includes honoring the Dragonsisters, recommending Draygar, questioning the aftermath of battle and offering himself as a model for the city after Aria’s death.

The war he carries

On 15, Month of Cala, Year 2, Zythienne introduces himself to the celebration as Captain Z, the name his soldiers use. He speaks of victory, peace and horizons opening beyond Zarathis’s shores. His ambition is expansive: he wants his people’s prosperity carried into lands broken by the Void.

In the same speech he says he has lost his own son, and that he and his wife still cry at night. He promises to stand on the front line with Aria during a planned final assault and asks forgiveness for the soldiers he loses. The loss and promise are his public testimony; the proposed assault is still ahead of the speech.

You cannot lead if you cannot risk.Captain Zythienne

A guest later tells Eldin that the captain obtained excellent healing for an injured daughter and visited her himself. That witness’s gratitude belongs beside the captain’s rhetoric. He is admired for care as well as for command.

Making hidden service public

Zythienne calls Sheeva, Kaiya and Minyah before the crowd and credits their years of work among the enemy. He singles out Sheeva for discovering that captives were being fed to dragons. His estimate of five years describes the length of their service without establishing an exact starting date.

He announces that the sisters will be ladies of the land and that their families will be honored and cared for over generations. The ceremony turns covert work into public recognition. It does not by itself specify estates, legal powers or military commands for the sisters.

Zythienne pays for the gathering from his own coffers, according to his address. Yet celebration and unfinished danger coexist: he also says the enemy’s holy temple remains protected by sacrificial wards. His confidence in the coming assault is not a completed victory at the time he speaks.

Recognition after the battle

At the gathering on 5, Month of Moirah, the narrator places Zythienne beside High Lord Bowene. Draygar approaches, and the captain tells him that he fought well. He remembers the initial charge and offers to recommend him to Captain Tarwen of the Silver Star.

Their conversation makes duty more specific. Draygar wants to protect people who cannot protect themselves; Zythienne asks whether teaching others to fight might lift them up as well. He values the same honor while challenging how it should be put into practice. The recommendation is offered and a letter is promised; this exchange alone does not establish its delivery or a new appointment.

His immediate concern is the enormous creature that appeared in the battle and killed soldiers. Before hearing the public account, he wants to know whether it is a threat. During the gathering he remains watchful, scanning the crowd with a composed face rather than displaying every reaction.

What trust cannot settle

After the hearing, Draygar tells him that incompatible testimony makes him fear dishonor. Zythienne initially asks where the dishonor lies: both speakers, he says, were under an effect that compelled truth. When Draygar presses the contradiction, the captain accepts that both accounts cannot be true.

His difficulty then becomes more personal and cultural. He says he cannot easily look past Adelia’s admitted use of divine power, because the gods once ruined his people. He invokes the Silver Star’s memory. Draygar answers that he has seen that power used for protection as well as harm and praises Adelia’s conduct.

The exchange leaves disagreement visible. Zythienne’s trust in the truth-telling effect does not independently resolve the battle’s history, and his fear of divine interference does not prove that the outsiders intended betrayal. Read the wider history of Zarathian judgment →

Preparation before another war

At the council on 26, Month of Death, Year 2, Zythienne says troops can be trained and weapons forged to hurt the heavenly host. He also wants information: where the enemy is, and what the battlefield will be like.

He proposes sending a small group of experts through the Void to scout, so that a whole army need not linger there without direction. Scribonia offers help while warning that the passage is unstable and dangerous, and that transporting troops and war machines could cost lives. The scene establishes preparation and a request for reconnaissance, not a guaranteed safe route or a completed campaign.

Read the full war council →

The excellence he offers the city

After Aria’s death, Zythienne enters the leadership gathering with military dignity and offers himself as an example of Zarathian excellence. He says he represents the city on the battlefield, in the courtroom and in the amphitheater. Skill with the brush and with words belongs in his self-description alongside the blade.

Arandiel, his political rival, acknowledges his service while drawing her own contrast between a commander and someone who fights. That is an argument for her candidacy, not independent proof that he never risked himself. Zythienne’s reply to the city is to emphasize inspiration, discipline and a refusal to settle for being merely good enough. Bowene praises his excellence.

The speeches establish a candidate, not his election to Aria’s symbolic position or the transfer of Bowene’s office. Later, in the Month of War, Year 3, Lucent reports that he and Tarwen have personally overseen the care of survivors from a newly arrived ship. Her account places his service beyond the war speeches without inventing a new office for him.

Evidence and limits

Zythienne’s speeches show how he wants his command understood. Draygar’s conversation and a guest’s account of care for an injured soldier offer other views. The difference between a public promise, a witness’s judgment and a later report remains visible.

The open record

The surviving scenes do not establish the complete structure of his command, the exact circumstances of his son’s death, delivery of Draygar’s recommendation, or every later military assignment. His speeches, his conduct in a tense crowd and other people’s judgments give different views of the same officer.
